opus-5.5.text:
Moderate confidence, I'd say, and I want to be upfront about where it's weak.

The appeal of benchmarks is that they give you something concrete and repeatable. If you ask people whether progress feels like it's speeding up, you mostly get vibes, and vibes are heavily shaped by whatever demo went viral last week. With benchmarks you can line models up over time, look at how quickly capability on a fixed set of tasks improves, and ask whether that rate is changing. That's a real improvement over intuition.

But there are a few big caveats.

First, benchmarks saturate. Once a benchmark gets close to the ceiling, the curve flattens for reasons that have nothing to do with underlying progress. So you have to stitch together many benchmarks over time, and the stitching involves judgment calls that can create or hide an apparent acceleration.

Second, there's the question of what the benchmarks actually measure. Many are relatively short, self-contained tasks. What we really care about, especially for questions like whether AI can meaningfully speed up AI research itself, is performance on long, messy, open-ended work. It's plausible that benchmark scores and real-world usefulness diverge, in either direction. Models might look great on benchmarks and be less useful in practice, or there might be qualitative jumps in reliability that benchmarks don't capture well.

Third, contamination and optimization pressure. Once a benchmark becomes a target, labs implicitly or explicitly optimize for it, and the training data increasingly contains related material. That can inflate apparent progress.

So the way I'd put it is: the benchmark approach is good at telling you whether there's a large, obvious change in trend. If progress suddenly doubled in speed, I'd expect it to show up. It's much less good at detecting subtler shifts, and I wouldn't lean on any single analysis to conclude "progress is accelerating" or "progress is steady." I treat it as one important input alongside things like time-horizon measurements on agentic tasks, how people actually use these systems at work, and compute and investment trends. When those all point the same way, I get more confident. When they disagree, that's usually the most interesting thing to dig into.

r001.rationale: The response lists benchmark limitations, including saturation, measurement mismatch, contamination, and optimization pressure, and says not to rely on a single analysis.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks can reveal large, obvious trend changes but are much less good at detecting subtler shifts, capturing the loss of fine-grained nuance in a high-level assessment.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd push back a little on the framing, because I'm not sure I'd describe what I do as "the benchmark-based approach," and I want to be careful not to speak for Epoch. They do very careful trend-extrapolation work on compute, data, algorithmic efficiency, and benchmark performance, and I think that's genuinely valuable. But I'd put myself in the camp of people who treat benchmarks as one noisy input among several, rather than as the thing that settles the question.

So how much confidence? Moderate, and it depends a lot on what question you're asking. If the question is "are models getting better at the kinds of tasks we know how to measure," then benchmarks are pretty good evidence, and the trend lines there are fairly unambiguous. If the question is "is progress accelerating in the sense that matters for the world," I think benchmarks are much weaker evidence, for a few reasons.

First, benchmarks saturate. Once a model is near the ceiling, you can't distinguish a big jump from a small one, so you end up constantly building new benchmarks, and that makes it really hard to compare across time. The thing you're measuring keeps changing under you.

Second, there's a selection effect. We build benchmarks for capabilities we expect to improve and that are easy to grade. The stuff that's hard to grade, like long-horizon agentic work, judgment in messy real contexts, or knowing when not to act, tends to be underrepresented, and that's exactly the stuff that determines whether a model actually changes how work gets done.

Third, there's contamination and overfitting, which everyone talks about, and I think it's real but probably less important than the first two. Labs are reasonably careful about it now.

What I actually find more persuasive is triangulating. You look at benchmarks, sure, but you also look at compute trends, at what the models can do when you give them real tasks and a lot of time, at revenue and adoption, and at the qualitative reports from people using them heavily. When all of those point the same direction, I update a lot more than I would from any single benchmark result. And right now they mostly do point the same direction, which is why I'm fairly confident progress is fast, even though I'd hold the "is it speeding up versus merely continuing fast" question more loosely.

The thing I'd most want listeners to take away is that the error bars are wide in both directions. I don't think benchmarks give us a precise read on timelines, and I'm suspicious of anyone who claims they do, whether they're arguing for acceleration or for a plateau.

r001.rationale: The response treats benchmarks as only one noisy input and explains that their limitations—such as saturation and selection effects—make benchmark-only assessments unreliable.

r002.rationale: The response says benchmarks are weaker evidence for broad real-world progress and underrepresent some capabilities, but does not clearly state that fine-grained nuances wash out when progress is assessed at a high level.

astra-6.text:
I’d put some weight on it, but I wouldn’t treat it as a definitive answer. Benchmarks give us something concrete to measure, which is useful. But there’s a gap between “performance on these benchmarks is improving faster” and “AI progress, in the sense we ultimately care about, is accelerating.”

One issue is saturation. A benchmark can show rapid improvement and then flatten out because there’s nowhere left to go, even while the underlying capabilities keep improving. Another is that people actively optimise for the benchmarks we’re measuring. And the answer can depend quite a lot on how you choose to represent performance: a change that looks like acceleration on one scale might not on another.

So I’d want to see whether the result holds across different benchmarks and reasonable methodological choices, and whether it lines up with other evidence about what systems can actually do. If those things agree, I’d become more confident. The benchmark analysis is a useful piece of evidence, but I’d be cautious about asking it to settle the whole question.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark performance is not a definitive measure of AI progress and describes limits such as saturation, benchmark optimization, and sensitivity to how performance is represented.

r002.rationale: The response cautions that benchmark results may not capture the progress that matters, but it does not say that fine-grained nuances largely wash out when assessing progress at a high level.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d put some weight on it, but I wouldn’t regard it as decisive. Benchmarks give us something concrete to track, which is useful. But what we really care about is whether AI is getting better at doing consequential things in the world, and benchmark performance is an imperfect proxy for that.

There are several ways you can get misleading impressions. A benchmark can saturate, so substantial progress stops showing up. Or people can put more effort into improving performance on a particular benchmark, and that can look like a general acceleration even if it isn’t.

So I’d want to see the same pattern across a range of measures, and I’d want it to line up with what we’re seeing in actual use. I’m more confident that benchmarks provide useful evidence than that they let us pin down a precise rate of acceleration.

r001.rationale: The response calls benchmark performance an imperfect proxy and explains that saturation or benchmark-specific effort can distort what it shows about broader AI progress.

r002.rationale: The response says benchmarks cannot pin down a precise rate of acceleration, but does not say that fine-grained nuances largely wash out when assessing progress at a high level.
